The root limit is 0.6, so the series converges only if the terms shrink faster than that.
options.misconception: confuses the root limit with a required decay rate

questions.explanation: Every reported root value is below 1 and the series of them is drifting slowly upwards, so the root limit is below 1 and the root test indicates convergence.
questions.hint: Compare every listed value with 1.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.topic: Sum of an alternating geometric series
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an infinite alternating geometric series.
questions.stem: Ticket BATCH-9043 asks the batch service for the value of the infinite series 3 - 3/4 + 3/16 - 3/64 + 3/256 - ... used in a rounding correction.
questions.explanation: The first term is 3 and the ratio is -1/4, so the sum is 3/(1 + 1/4) = 12/5 = 2.4. Taking the absolute value of the ratio would give the sum of the absolute terms instead.
questions.hint: Use a = 3 and r = -1/4 in the geometric formula.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.topic: Absolute versus conditional convergence
questions.learningObjective: Justify absolute convergence by examining absolute values.
questions.stem: A claim in a design note says the series 1 - 1/4 + 1/9 - 1/16 + ... converges absolutely, and the reviewer asks for the justification.

options.text: Taking absolute values gives 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + ..., a convergent p-series with p equal to two.
Taking absolute values gives 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ..., which is the harmonic series and so diverges.
options.misconception: mistakes square denominators for consecutive ones

options.text: Taking absolute values gives 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + ..., but the summands grow so the sum cannot exist.
options.misconception: believes reciprocals of squares grow

options.text: Taking absolute values gives the same series, so the absolute and signed sums agree term by term.
options.misconception: thinks absolute values leave the terms unchanged

questions.explanation: The absolute values are 1, 1/4, 1/9, 1/16, which is a p-series with p = 2 and therefore converges. The claim in the design note is correct, and the harmonic series is not what appears here.
questions.hint: Write the series of absolute values and identify it.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.topic: The ratio test for a positive-term series
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a ratio above one forces divergence.
questions.stem: An apprentice asks why a positive-term series can be shown divergent by showing that the ratio of consecutive terms exceeds 1 eventually.

options.text: Because a ratio above 1 makes the terms shrink geometrically, so the sum of the terms is finite.
options.misconception: reverses the effect of a ratio above one

options.text: Because a ratio above 1 makes the terms grow, so the partial sums cannot approach a finite limit.
Because a ratio above 1 means the series is a p-series with p above one, which diverges.
options.misconception: invents a p-series reading of a ratio limit

options.text: Because a ratio above 1 only rules out geometric series, and other series may still converge.
options.misconception: believes the test applies only to geometric series

questions.explanation: If each term is a fixed multiple greater than 1 of the one before, the terms grow without bound and the partial sums run away.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the terms themselves.

questions.topic: The exponential series and a power of e
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a column of partial sums of the exponential series.
questions.stem: A spreadsheet evaluates the exponential series at x equal to two, listing the partial sums 1, 3, 5, 6.3333, 7, 7.2667, 7.3556, and the column keeps filling in.

options.text: The column approaches 3, because the growth of the partial sums slows down and then stops.
options.misconception: believes slowing growth implies a small limit

options.text: The column approaches 6.3333, because that is the largest meaningful partial sum listed.
options.misconception: stops the series at a convenient point

options.text: The column approaches 7, because the terms beyond the fourth contribute less than a third.
options.misconception: ignores the later terms of the series

options.text: The column approaches 7.38906, the value of e squared, which is the limit of this series.

questions.explanation: The listed values are the partial sums of the Taylor series of e raised to the power 2, whose limit is 7.38906.
questions.hint: Identify the input and the function being expanded.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.topic: The root test and its three cases
questions.learningObjective: State the root test verdict in the boundary case.
questions.stem: A final review item asks the team to state the verdict of the root test when the limit of the nth roots of the terms equals one exactly.

options.text: The root test proves the series converges, because a limit of one means the terms are harmless.
options.misconception: treats the boundary case as a convergence verdict

options.text: The root test is inconclusive, because a limit of one separates the convergent case from the divergent one.
The root test proves the series diverges, because a limit of one means the terms stop shrinking.
options.misconception: treats the boundary case as a divergence verdict

options.text: The root test proves the series converges, because a limit of one is smaller than any limit above one.
options.misconception: compares the limit with the wrong reference value

questions.explanation: A root limit exactly equal to 1 is the boundary case, and the root test then says nothing. Series such as the harmonic and the p-series with p = 2 both sit at that boundary and behave differently.
questions.hint: Recall the third case of the root test.
